one_liner: Drive STM32 GPIO pins with single stores to the BSRR register instead of calling HAL_GPIO_WritePin.
what_it_does: A coding technique, not a library: the book's companion code writes peripheral registers through CMSIS-style structs (GPIOA->MODER, GPIOA->BSRR, RCC->AHB1ENR) on an STM32F411 NUCLEO board, with its own startup file, linker script and CMSIS headers, and builds GPIO, timer, UART, SPI, I2C, ADC and DMA drivers that way. Setting or clearing a pin becomes one 32-bit store (GPIOx->BSRR = 1u<<n to set, 1u<<(n+16) to clear) in place of the HAL call. There is no drop-in API: the caller enables clocks, configures MODER/OSPEEDR and owns every register bit.
how_it_is_fast: BSRR is a write-only set/reset register, so one store changes the pin atomically with no read-modify-write and no function call. In the measured loop the HAL cost is call overhead, not work: the F0 HAL_GPIO_WritePin body is just a branch and one store to BSRR or BRR (assert_param compiles to nothing with USE_FULL_ASSERT off), but it lives in a separate driver file and the Keil project has LTO off, so each write pays a call and return. The 40.8 ns BSRR pulse is about 2 cycles at 48 MHz, which the benchmark author reads as the Cortex-M0 store timing limit.
when_to_use: Bit-banged protocols, chip-select or strobe lines and scope/debug markers where the gap between two pin edges must be a few CPU cycles.
Interrupt handlers and tight control loops on STM32 parts that already use CMSIS device headers, where a HAL call per pin edge is measurable.
Setting or clearing pins from both main code and ISRs: a plain BSRR store is atomic, unlike ODR |= or ODR ^= read-modify-write sequences.
Learning or auditing exactly what the hardware does, or very small firmware images where HAL is not linked at all.
when_not_to_use: Code that must move across STM32 families or vendors: register names, bit positions and clock-enable registers differ (the book targets STM32F411, the benchmark STM32F072).
When LL (LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin is a static inline BSRR write) or HAL built with -O2 and LTO already meets the timing; the gap is mostly call overhead that inlining removes.
Peripheral setup and error handling: direct writes skip HAL's clock enabling, parameter checks, state machines and timeouts, so mistakes fail silently.
Workloads where a pin write is a tiny fraction of the time (pins toggled every few milliseconds); the saving is a few hundred nanoseconds per call.

integration.dependencies: CMSIS device header for the target MCU (the book repo ships chip_headers/CMSIS; the benchmark uses STM32CubeMX-generated CMSIS and HAL for setup)
integration.min_toolchain: Any C99 Arm compiler; book code built with the GNU Arm Embedded Toolchain in STM32CubeIDE, benchmark with Keil uVision5 and Arm Compiler 6
integration.platforms: STM32 MCUs with a BSRR GPIO register (book: STM32F411 Cortex-M4; benchmark: STM32F072 Cortex-M0); register layout is per family
integration.thread_safety: A single BSRR store is atomic with respect to interrupts; ODR read-modify-write forms used elsewhere in the book are not
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces HAL_GPIO_WritePin calls one for one, but pin masks, clock enabling and pin configuration must be written by hand

gotchas: The book's own GPIO driver (Chapter7-GpioInput/Src/gpio.c) writes GPIOA->BSRR |= LED_BS5, which adds a needless read of a write-only register; use a plain store as in the benchmark. Chapters 3 and 6 toggle with ODR ^=, which is not interrupt-safe.

The benchmark's HAL figures are call overhead across a translation-unit boundary with LTO off; its README attributes the -O0 gap to parameter validation and says HAL is inlined at -O2, but asserts are compiled out and HAL_GPIO_WritePin is a separate function in a non-LTO build.

Variants are switched by commenting code in main.c (the committed file has the HAL block active) and the Keil project stores a single optimization setting, so each table row was a separate hand-edited build; no build logs or disassembly are committed.
The book examples use empty for loops as delays (for(int i=0;i<100000;i++){}), which an optimizing compiler may delete; use SysTick or a timer instead.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick raw BSRR writes over the STM32 Low Layer (LL) entry only when you want no ST driver code at all; LL_GPIO_SetOutputPin compiles to the same single BSRR store when inlined, so LL gives the same edge timing with named calls and CubeMX support. The other filesystems-and-io siblings (liburing, SPDK, mmap replacements) solve host file and block I/O and do not apply to microcontroller pins.
verified_claims_summary: A third-party student project (dotsolvit/stm32f0-gpio-speed-comparison) toggled PC8 on an STM32F072 Discovery board at 48 MHz, built with Keil and Arm Compiler 6, and measured the high-pulse width with an OWON SDS210S oscilloscope: two HAL_GPIO_WritePin calls gave 396 ns at -O2/-O3 versus 40.8 ns for two GPIOC->BSRR stores (9.7x), 418 versus 61.6 ns at -O1 and 896 versus 61.6 ns at -O0. The book and its repository contain no timing; the measurement is of the technique on a different chip, not of the book's code.
status_note: The book repository (MIT, 317 stars, last commit 2025-12-15, 4 open issues about errata and tooling) is teaching code for STM32F411, small enough to copy; the benchmark repository has no license file and 0 stars, so cite its numbers but do not copy its code.
